title: TCL
description: Control transactional row changes with START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT, while distinguishing session ownership, autocommit, statement errors, and implicit commits.
notes:
## Choosing a transaction boundary

Transaction Control Language, or TCL, names SQL operations that manage transaction boundaries. COMMIT completes the current transaction successfully, while ROLLBACK discards the transactional changes still pending in it. SAVEPOINT introduces a named position for a partial rollback within a transaction. These operations make sense only with the actual engine, connection, and statement behavior in view.

This topic uses MySQL 8.4 and transactional InnoDB fixtures. It does not assume that every storage engine or every SQL operation can be rolled back. Temporary objects are created before the exercise transaction begins, and the exercises change synthetic rows only. No application migration, permission, or production record is modified by the lesson.

A transaction represents a chosen unit of work, not merely every statement written near another in a source file. The caller must establish the intended boundary and keep its statements on the correct session. A group of unrelated connections cannot become one transaction simply because an application calls them in sequence.

## Understanding the need for atomic work

The familiar transfer illustration debits one account and credits another. The intended outcome is both valid effects together or neither, rather than a permanent debit without its corresponding credit. A transaction provides a boundary within which those changes can be committed together, provided the operation uses a transactional engine and handles failure correctly.

That description is not a complete financial implementation. Account authorization, sufficient funds, concurrent updates, currencies, and duplicate requests require trusted rules beyond the mere presence of START TRANSACTION. A caller that ignores an error and commits the earlier successful debit can still produce an invalid partial business operation. The application must follow the failure policy the operation actually needs.

Use the same reasoning for a simpler supply fixture. A stock reallocation can involve a decrease in one row and an increase in another. The quantity rules and chosen transaction boundary should make the intended final state explicit. Test the rejected and rolled-back cases as well as a successful pair of writes.

## Starting and completing an explicit transaction

START TRANSACTION begins an explicit transaction on the current connection. Successful statements can then contribute uncommitted changes. COMMIT ends that transaction with its accepted effects, while a full ROLLBACK abandons pending transactional changes. A later transaction is a separate unit; its rollback does not normally undo earlier committed work.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE stock SET quantity = quantity + 2 WHERE item_id = 1;
COMMIT;
```

For an initial quantity of three, the committed result is five. The example assumes the row exists and the update is valid. A missing target requires its own operation policy rather than an automatic claim that the intended business action succeeded. Inspect the appropriate affected-row behavior and trusted checks in the real implementation.

The client must also interpret confirmation carefully. If the connection fails around commit, the caller may not know whether the server completed it. Reconnecting does not establish that the earlier write rolled back. Blindly repeating an additive change can apply it twice, so uncertain outcomes need a defined retry or reconciliation strategy.

## Rolling back pending changes

A full ROLLBACK ends the current transaction and discards its pending transactional changes. If an exercise begins with quantity three, updates it to zero, and then rolls back before commit, the later read should show three again. The expected state is the earlier valid value, not a new value inferred from an abandoned assignment.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE stock SET quantity = 0 WHERE item_id = 1;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT item_id, quantity FROM stock ORDER BY item_id;
```

Do not generalize this to every possible effect. Nontransactional storage and operations causing implicit commits can fall outside that rollback scope. External messages or other services also do not automatically reverse themselves because database rows rolled back. Define the full workflow's guarantees separately from the local row transaction.

Statement errors need precise handling. An error can reject one statement while leaving earlier changes pending, depending on the failure and engine rules. Other failures can end a broader transaction scope. The caller must inspect the actual behavior and finish or abandon the intended unit explicitly instead of treating every exception as proof that no work remains.

## Using a savepoint for partial rollback

A SAVEPOINT marks a position inside an open transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT can discard changes after that marker while keeping earlier work pending. The transaction remains open; the partial rollback is not a commit of what came before. Later completion still determines whether retained pending changes become committed.

For example, add two to item 1, mark after_primary, then try a provisional five-unit increase for item 2. Rolling back to after_primary removes the provisional increase but retains the earlier change to item 1. A later COMMIT accepts the retained change. This is useful when the workflow explicitly allows abandoning a sub-operation without abandoning everything.

A savepoint is not an independently committed nested transaction. Releasing a savepoint removes the marker rather than making earlier changes permanent. A later full ROLLBACK can still discard retained pending work. Savepoint names and lifetime follow the database's supported behavior, so do not infer unlimited nested transaction semantics from a convenient marker.

## Interpreting autocommit correctly

MySQL connections commonly operate with autocommit enabled. Outside an explicit transaction, a successful transactional statement can complete as its own unit. That means a later ROLLBACK is not a time machine for every earlier statement the connection executed. The intended multi-statement boundary must be established before the related operations.

Autocommit is connection state. It does not prove that every connection in an application has the same current settings, especially when pooling or middleware participates. A borrowed session may require documented reset behavior so one request does not inherit an unfinished transaction or surprising setting from another.

An explicit transaction groups supported work under the relevant rules even when the normal connection mode commits individual statements. Use the established driver transaction helper or supported SQL controls consistently. Starting transaction control through one pooled handle and sending the updates through unrelated convenience calls can scatter the work across different sessions.

## Keeping DDL behavior separate

Many ordinary permanent MySQL DDL operations cause implicit commits. Interleaving one into a row transaction can end the boundary the application thought it still controlled. A later ROLLBACK cannot be assumed to undo both the definition change and every earlier row operation. Check the exact statement, engine, and version.

Temporary-table creation has its own distinction: it avoids the usual CREATE TABLE implicit commit but is not itself undone by user rollback. The exercises create their required objects before the transaction and test transactional row behavior, rather than pretending temporary object lifetime and row rollback are the same concept.

Other products can support different transactional DDL behavior. In particular, a blanket statement that SQL Server cannot roll back CREATE TABLE is incorrect. The safe teaching rule is to verify the specific operation on the intended engine. A MariaDB compatibility run provides evidence for its executed fixture, not exact MySQL or hosted-provider semantics.

## Managing locks and session lifetime

An open transaction can retain locks or other resources and block unrelated work even while the application is idle. It can also keep a visibility context alive. The exact consequences depend on what it did and the configured engine and isolation behavior, so not every idle transaction has identical locks or costs.

Keep transaction duration tied to the required unit. Avoid holding a borrowed connection and open transaction while waiting for unrelated user interaction or a slow external service unless the design deliberately accounts for it. On success, error, cancellation, and early return, the caller needs a clear completion and cleanup policy.

Returning an unfinished transaction to a pool can let later work inherit unexpected state. A clean network connection is not proof of a clean transactional context. Inspect the actual pool and driver lifecycle, and test failure paths that bypass the ordinary success return. Resource reuse should preserve the transaction contract rather than conceal who owns it.

## Verifying boundaries through final state

For each fixture, state the initial rows, the requested changes, the transaction controls, and the exact ordered final result. Include missing targets, untouched rows, full rollback, partial rollback, and a valid commit. A final state check can demonstrate which effects survived, while separate rejected-input checks verify the declared validity rules.

TCL is most useful when it makes ownership and completion explicit. Keep pending changes distinct from committed ones, savepoint rollback distinct from a full rollback, and transactional row behavior distinct from structural or external effects. Those distinctions support reliable SQL examples without promising that a transaction keyword alone supplies business correctness, authorization, or universal recovery.

questions.question_text: What does COMMIT do for a valid current InnoDB transaction?
options: ROLLBACK
It completes the transaction and accepts its pending transactional effects
SAVEPOINT
GRANT
questions.explanation: Durability and confirmation still depend on the actual engine and operational guarantees.

questions.question_text: What does a full ROLLBACK discard in the current transaction?
options: COMMIT
Its pending transactional changes, not every earlier committed or nontransactional effect
REVOKE
ALTER
questions.explanation: The scope is transactional work still pending in the current boundary.

questions.question_text: Why group the debit and credit of a transfer under a correct transaction and failure policy?
options: To make the query run faster
To commit both valid effects together or roll back the intended unit when it cannot complete
Because SQL requires every UPDATE to be paired with another UPDATE
To avoid needing a WHERE clause
questions.explanation: The application must handle errors and enforce the full trusted business rules; keywords alone are insufficient.

questions.question_text: What does a SAVEPOINT let you do that plain COMMIT/ROLLBACK cannot?
options: Permanently save data even without ever committing
Mark an intermediate point inside a longer transaction that you can roll back to, without discarding the whole transaction
Grant privileges to another user
Create a new table
questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback to a marked point, rather than an all-or-nothing rollback of the entire transaction.

questions.question_text: What does 'auto-commit mode' mean for a database connection?
options: Every statement automatically becomes part of one giant, permanent transaction that never ends
Each individual statement is implicitly wrapped in and completed by its own commit, unless an explicit transaction is started
COMMIT is disabled entirely in auto-commit mode
Auto-commit mode disables all DML statements
questions.explanation: In auto-commit mode (the common default), each statement commits on its own; an explicit BEGIN groups multiple statements into one atomic unit instead.

questions.question_text: Which ACID property does TCL most directly implement and control at the SQL level?
options: Atomicity
Consistency alone, with no relation to atomicity
Only Durability
None of the ACID properties relate to TCL
questions.explanation: TCL's all-or-nothing COMMIT/ROLLBACK model is specifically how atomicity — one of the four ACID guarantees — is expressed and controlled via SQL.

questions.question_text: Why can a long-running, idle-but-open transaction be an operational hazard even if it never gets rolled back?
options: It has no real cost as long as it is eventually committed
It can continue holding locks and blocking other work the whole time it stays open, regardless of whether the application is actively using it
Open transactions automatically time out and self-commit after one second
Idle transactions consume no database resources at all
questions.explanation: Held locks from an open transaction can block other sessions for as long as the transaction remains open, whether or not it's doing active work — a real, easy-to-overlook cost.

questions.question_text: Can ROLLBACK be assumed to undo any DDL operation on any database?
options: Yes, this is guaranteed identically on every SQL database
No; implicit-commit and rollback behavior depend on the exact product, engine, and operation
ROLLBACK only ever affects SELECT statements
DDL statements cannot appear inside a transaction on any engine
questions.explanation: This avoids the incorrect universal SQL Server claim in the retained question.

questions.question_text: Does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT commit the changes before the marker?
options: Yes; it always commits them
No; retained changes remain pending in the open transaction
Only on the first connection
Only if the marker name is short
questions.explanation: Partial rollback and successful transaction completion are distinct.

questions.question_text: Why keep all statements of the ordinary session-based transaction on the intended connection?
options: Every session shares one global transaction
Pooling disables all state
The transaction context belongs to that session
Consecutive API calls always use the same connection
questions.explanation: A sequence of calls can otherwise use unrelated transactional contexts.

questions.question_text: Quantity 3 is changed to 0 and then rolled back before commit in the fixture. What is the final quantity?
questions.explanation: The uncommitted row change is discarded.

questions.question_text: Item 1 is increased before a savepoint; item 2 is increased after it. ROLLBACK TO that marker then COMMIT occurs. Which increase survives?
options: Both increases
Only item 2's later increase
Neither because savepoints always remove earlier work
Only item 1's earlier increase
questions.explanation: The partial rollback removes the later change and the commit accepts the retained one.

questions.question_text: A savepoint is released and a full ROLLBACK follows. What should not be assumed?
options: That releasing the marker committed earlier pending changes
That the transaction has a lifecycle
That a marker can be removed
That rollback scope matters
questions.explanation: Releasing a savepoint is not a subtransaction commit.

questions.question_text: An autocommitted update succeeded long before ROLLBACK is issued. What is unsafe to expect?
options: That the successful update had a boundary
That the later rollback reverses that completed statement
That actual session mode matters
That explicit transactions can group work
questions.explanation: A later rollback does not undo arbitrary previous commits.

questions.question_text: A later statement errors but earlier writes remain pending. What must the caller do?
options: Assume every earlier statement vanished
Return the connection unfinished
Apply the intended failure policy and complete or roll back the correct unit
Report unconditional success
questions.explanation: Statement failure and full transaction rollback can have different scopes.

questions.question_text: The commit response is lost and the client reconnects. What remains uncertain?
options: Whether a new session can exist
Whether the caller lacked a timely response
Whether errors need handling
Whether the earlier transaction committed
questions.explanation: A new connection does not resolve the previous commit outcome.

questions.question_text: A permanent MySQL DDL statement is inserted into a row transaction. What boundary risk arises?
options: It may cause an implicit commit
It always creates a nested transaction
It makes all old commits reversible
It prevents every future SELECT
questions.explanation: The exact operation can end an assumed transaction boundary.

questions.question_text: An open transaction becomes idle after holding locks. Why can it still matter?
options: Idle always means resource-free
It can retain resources and block other work
It automatically commits after one second
Locks only exist while the UI animates
questions.explanation: Transaction lifetime can outlast active statement execution.

questions.question_text: A connection returns to a pool with an unfinished transaction. What needs correction?
options: Only the connection's variable name
Only the result table heading
Ownership, completion, and supported reset/cleanup behavior
Only query indentation
questions.explanation: Later borrowers must not inherit unexpected pending state.

questions.question_text: A database rollback occurs after an external message was sent. What cannot automatically be inferred?
options: That local transactional changes may be discarded
That the operation has multiple effects
That a workflow contract is needed
That the external message was undone
questions.explanation: Other systems do not automatically participate in the local rollback.

coding_problems.title: Discard a provisional stock reset
coding_problems.task: Start a transaction, set quantity to 0 for item_id 1, and roll back that transaction. Return item_id, quantity for all stock rows ordered by item_id. The provided InnoDB fixture is established before your transaction.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE stock (item_id INT PRIMARY KEY, quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0)) ENGINE=InnoDB;
constraints: Do not create or alter objects inside the transaction
edge_cases: Missing item 1 leaves other rows unchanged
hints: Use full ROLLBACK before the final SELECT
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Begin, update the target, roll back, then read final rows.
coding_problems.explanation: The final read occurs after rollback, so the provisional transactional update does not replace the fixture quantity. The output check alone cannot prove a student used transaction controls; the reference script is executed and reviewed.

coding_problems.title: Commit an earlier change after partial rollback
coding_problems.task: Start a transaction. Add 2 to quantity for item_id 1, set a savepoint named after_primary, add 5 to item_id 2, roll back to after_primary, and commit. Return item_id, quantity for all rows ordered by item_id. Preserve unrelated stock rows.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE stock (item_id INT PRIMARY KEY, quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0)) ENGINE=InnoDB;
constraints: No structural or implicit-commit operation inside the transaction
edge_cases: Missing item 1 must not change the item 2 rollback policy
hints: Create the savepoint after the first update
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT keeps the transaction open
COMMIT the retained work before reading
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Use both full transaction completion and a partial rollback marker.
coding_problems.explanation: The marker follows the first increment. Partial rollback discards the later increment while leaving the earlier one pending, and COMMIT accepts the retained change. Output fixtures validate final state; exact use of the required controls also needs source review.

original_questions.question_text: Which TCL statement makes all changes in the current transaction permanent?
options: ROLLBACK
COMMIT
SAVEPOINT
GRANT
original_questions.explanation: COMMIT finalizes and makes permanent every change made since the transaction began.

original_questions.question_text: Which TCL statement undoes all changes made since the transaction began?
options: COMMIT
ROLLBACK
REVOKE
ALTER
original_questions.explanation: ROLLBACK discards every change made in the current transaction, as if it never ran.

original_questions.question_text: In the classic bank-transfer example (debit one account, credit another), why must both UPDATEs be in one transaction?
options: To make the query run faster
So that if only one of the two UPDATEs succeeds, the whole operation can be rolled back instead of leaving money debited from one account but never credited to the other
Because SQL requires every UPDATE to be paired with another UPDATE
To avoid needing a WHERE clause
original_questions.explanation: Wrapping both statements in one transaction guarantees atomicity — either both happen or neither does, preventing money from vanishing.

original_questions.question_text: What does a SAVEPOINT let you do that plain COMMIT/ROLLBACK cannot?
options: Permanently save data even without ever committing
Mark an intermediate point inside a longer transaction that you can roll back to, without discarding the whole transaction
Grant privileges to another user
Create a new table
original_questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback to a marked point, rather than an all-or-nothing rollback of the entire transaction.

original_questions.question_text: What does 'auto-commit mode' mean for a database connection?
options: Every statement automatically becomes part of one giant, permanent transaction that never ends
Each individual statement is implicitly wrapped in and completed by its own commit, unless an explicit transaction is started
COMMIT is disabled entirely in auto-commit mode
Auto-commit mode disables all DML statements
original_questions.explanation: In auto-commit mode (the common default), each statement commits on its own; an explicit BEGIN groups multiple statements into one atomic unit instead.

original_questions.question_text: Which ACID property does TCL most directly implement and control at the SQL level?
options: Atomicity
Consistency alone, with no relation to atomicity
Only Durability
None of the ACID properties relate to TCL
original_questions.explanation: TCL's all-or-nothing COMMIT/ROLLBACK model is specifically how atomicity — one of the four ACID guarantees — is expressed and controlled via SQL.

original_questions.question_text: Why can a long-running, idle-but-open transaction be an operational hazard even if it never gets rolled back?
options: It has no real cost as long as it is eventually committed
It can continue holding locks and blocking other work the whole time it stays open, regardless of whether the application is actively using it
Open transactions automatically time out and self-commit after one second
Idle transactions consume no database resources at all
original_questions.explanation: Held locks from an open transaction can block other sessions for as long as the transaction remains open, whether or not it's doing active work — a real, easy-to-overlook cost.

original_questions.question_text: Is it safe to assume that ROLLBACK will always undo a DDL statement (like CREATE TABLE) that ran earlier in the same transaction, on any database engine?
options: Yes, this is guaranteed identically on every SQL database
No — whether DDL can be rolled back at all is engine-dependent (true on PostgreSQL, generally false on MySQL/Oracle/SQL Server), so this assumption is a portability trap
ROLLBACK only ever affects SELECT statements
DDL statements cannot appear inside a transaction on any engine
original_questions.explanation: As covered under DDL, whether DDL is transactional (rollback-able) varies significantly by engine — assuming uniform behavior here is a common portability mistake.
